subtype: Approach: forms a hypothesis, sets a measure and runs a small test [Thinking]
passage:
Mahima here. I help at the film club's table, so I watched Eshaan's little experiment. "My guess: posters bring more people than the group message," Eshaan said, writing it on the whiteboard. "To check, I put posters up in week one and send no message. Week two, only the group message and no posters. Then I count heads at the door both times, same day, same room."

Week one, nineteen people came. Week two, thirty-one. Eshaan looked at the two numbers for a while. "So my guess was wrong, for this club anyway. But two weeks is small. I'll do it once more with the order swapped." I cannot tell how Eshaan felt about being wrong, but the pen kept moving.

qa.q: How many people came in week two?
qa.a: Thirty-one people came in week two.

qa.q: What might Eshaan have felt on seeing that the guess was wrong?
qa.a: Eshaan may have felt a little disappointed but curious, since the pen kept moving and a repeat was planned, though Mahima cannot be sure.

qa.q: What could Eshaan do to make the test fairer?
qa.a: Eshaan could repeat it with the order swapped, as planned, and choose similar events so that the film or the day does not explain the difference.

qa.q: Why is Mahima careful about describing Eshaan's feelings?
qa.a: Mahima only saw what Eshaan said and did, such as the moving pen, so cannot know Eshaan's inner feelings for sure.

grounding: Shows a club organiser guessing that posters beat chat messages, trying each in a different week and counting who attends.

subtype: Approach: draws firm conclusions from too few results [Pitfall]
passage:
Dear Thomas,

Big news. I tried the flashcard-and-recall method you mentioned, for two days only, and my practice quiz went from 12 out of 20 on Monday to 14 on Wednesday. It works! I told the study group I'm skipping Friday's revision session because I don't need it now, and I recycled my old chemistry notes this morning. Some of the group said two days is too short to know, but I think they're just jealous. Wednesday's quiz was easier, to be honest, and I slept badly on Monday. Doesn't matter. Numbers don't lie. I'll show you my chart on Saturday.

Sachin

qa.q: What did the practice quiz score go to on Wednesday?
qa.a: The practice quiz went to 14 on Wednesday.

qa.q: What is Sachin feeling about the result?
qa.a: Sachin feels excited and very sure, so sure that the group's doubts are brushed aside.

qa.q: What could Sachin do to find out whether the method really works?
qa.a: Sachin could keep using it for a few more weeks, track several quizzes of similar difficulty and compare them with the old method, before dropping the notes or the group session.

qa.q: How might the study group feel about Sachin skipping Friday's session?
qa.a: The group may feel dismissed or worried, having said that two days is too short to know.

grounding: Shows a student declaring a new study method a success after two days of small improvement.

subtype: Approach: runs a pilot with a small group before a full rollout [Action]
passage:
Subject: Shift pilot proposal for Floor 2

Dear Joseph,

Before we change the roster for the whole floor, I would like to test it with one team first. Here is my plan. Team B, nine people, moves to the new pattern from the first of next month for four weeks. Team A stays as it is. Every week I will count absences and handover errors, meaning forms filled in wrongly or tasks missed at shift change, for both teams, and ask Team B one short question. At the end of the month I will bring you the numbers side by side, and we can decide whether to extend, adjust or drop the change. I would rather learn on nine people than on ninety.

Regards,
Minakshi

qa.q: How many people are in Team B?
qa.a: Team B has nine people.

qa.q: What does Minakshi hope to gain by running a pilot?
qa.a: Minakshi wants to learn from a small group first, so that any problems affect fewer people.

qa.q: What could Minakshi do if Team B's numbers improve only slightly?
qa.a: Minakshi could extend the pilot or ask Team B which part helped, before deciding about the whole floor.

qa.q: How might a Team B member feel about being in the pilot?
qa.a: A Team B member might feel curious or nervous about the new pattern, but the weekly question gives them a voice.

grounding: Shows a manager planning a month-long pilot with one team, tracking absences and handover errors, before wider use.

subtype: Approach: extends the trial and adds a comparison group after doubting the result [Revision]
passage:
Dear Thomas,

You may remember my triumphant note last week saying that focus blocks cut my evening emails by an hour a day. I did not sleep well on it. Three good days could just be a quiet week. So I carried on for four weeks and made week three a normal week without focus blocks, to compare. The result is less exciting: with the blocks I cleared my inbox about twenty minutes earlier each day, not an hour. But the plain week was clearly slower, so the gain is real, only smaller. I am still using the blocks and I have told the team the smaller number. Thank you for asking me how I knew.

Zainab

qa.q: How long did Zainab carry on with the trial?
qa.a: Zainab carried on for four weeks.

qa.q: What was Zainab worried about after the first three good days?
qa.a: Zainab worried that three good days could just be a quiet week, which is why doubt grew.

qa.q: What else could Zainab do to make the finding stronger?
qa.a: Zainab could ask a colleague to try the same routine as well, or repeat the comparison in a busier month.

qa.q: How might Thomas see Zainab's update?
qa.a: Thomas may be pleased that Zainab followed up honestly with the smaller number, since Thomas had asked how Zainab knew.

grounding: Shows a person doubting an early result, extending the trial with a comparison week and finding a smaller but real gain.

subtype: Approach: draws a picture of the problem to think through it [Action]
passage:
Tanuja sat on the veranda with her maths notebook while the goat next door chewed loudly. The sum said: twenty-three laddoos are shared equally among five children. How many does each child get, and how many are left? The numbers swam in her head.

"Draw it," said her brother Arnab, passing by with a bucket.

Tanuja drew five circles for the children. Then she made twenty-three dots for the laddoos and began putting one dot into each circle, round and round, crossing off dots as she went. After four rounds every circle held four dots. Three dots stood alone in the middle.

"Three left!" she said, and wrote the answer under her picture. Arnab looked, nodded and went on with his bucket.

qa.q: How many laddoos were shared, and among how many children?
qa.a: Twenty-three laddoos were shared equally among five children.

qa.q: How was Tanuja feeling before she drew the picture?
qa.a: Tanuja was confused and stuck, since the numbers swam in her head.

qa.q: How could Tanuja check her answer?
qa.a: Tanuja could count the dots in the circles and add the leftover ones to see whether they make twenty-three, or try it with real pebbles.

qa.q: How might Arnab see Tanuja's drawing?
qa.a: Arnab may feel pleased that the hint helped, since the drawing worked, as his nod suggests.

grounding: Shows a girl drawing circles for children and dots for sweets and reading the answer from the leftover dots.

subtype: Approach: writes a list to free up working memory [Action]
passage:
'Parth, why are you still awake?' Sabina asked from the doorway.

'Chemistry, maths, the physics file, the project, the library book...' Parth's voice cracked. 'Mummy, it's all in my head at once.'

'Then get it out of your head.' She put a notebook and pen in front of him. 'Write everything. Don't sort yet.'

Parth wrote for five minutes. Eleven lines. He stared at them. 'That's all?'

'That's all,' said Sabina. 'Now circle what has to happen tomorrow.'

He circled three. 'Chemistry chapter, the maths sheet and the file.'

'And the rest?'

'Later. The book goes back on Saturday.' He let out a long breath. 'It looks smaller on paper.'

'Sleep. The list will still be there in the morning.'

qa.q: How many lines did Parth write?
qa.a: Parth wrote eleven lines.

qa.q: How was Parth feeling when he could not sleep?
qa.a: Parth felt overwhelmed and worried, since everything was in his head at once.

qa.q: What else could Parth do the next morning with the list?
qa.a: Parth could put a time beside each item for today, or tick items off as they get done, so the list turns into a plan.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel watching Parth work through the list?
qa.a: Sabina may feel concerned at first and then relieved to see Parth calmer and ready to sleep.

grounding: Shows a student writing all tasks down, feeling less worried, and sorting them into today and later.

subtype: Approach: sketches a mind map to see how parts connect [Thinking]
passage:
Yusuf: Your thesis outline looks like a spider's web. Why draw it?

Kavitha: Because in a list everything looked separate. I drew boxes for each chapter, then boxes for my sources and my three questions, and arrows between them. While I was drawing the arrow from the survey data, I stopped, because a second arrow was already coming out of that same box. Chapter three and chapter five both rested on the same survey. If the survey came late, two chapters would freeze. I would never have seen that in a list.

Yusuf: What did you do?

Kavitha: I moved the survey to the top of my schedule and asked my supervisor to check the questionnaire this week.

qa.q: Which two chapters rested on the same survey?
qa.a: Chapter three and chapter five both rested on the same survey.

qa.q: What was Kavitha thinking when stopping at the second arrow?
qa.a: Kavitha suddenly realised that two chapters relied on one box, and worried that a late survey would freeze both.

qa.q: What could Kavitha do to reduce the risk of a late survey?
qa.a: Kavitha could put the survey first in the schedule, as Kavitha did, and keep a backup source ready in case it is delayed.

qa.q: How might Kavitha's supervisor see the diagram?
qa.a: The supervisor might find it useful for showing the risk and the plan, and be glad the questionnaire was checked early.

grounding: Shows a student drawing boxes and arrows for a thesis and noticing two chapters depend on the same data.

subtype: Approach: keeps writing notes without acting on them [Pitfall]
passage: Chetan, put that notebook down for a minute and listen to what Kiran did at your age. I wanted to open a small print shop, so I bought a notebook. Layouts, price lists, maps of the lane, a logo in six colours. Seven notebooks by the end of the year. Every night I closed the book and felt I had done a day's work. One day my uncle at the tea stall asked, "Which shop did you visit?" I had not visited one. I had not called a single supplier. The plans were beautiful and the door was still shut. A whole year gone with nothing begun, and the other print shop on the lane opened in March. Then I made one call. It was a clumsy call, but it was a call.

qa.q: How many notebooks had Kiran filled by the end of the year?
qa.a: Kiran had filled seven notebooks by the end of the year.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel each night when closing the notebook?
qa.a: Kiran felt satisfied, as if a day's work was done, though nothing had actually begun.

qa.q: Which moment in the story showed Kiran the missing first step?
qa.a: The uncle's question, "Which shop did you visit?", showed that no supplier had been called and no shop visited; a call after any evening of planning could have started things.

qa.q: How might the uncle at the tea stall have seen Kiran's plans?
qa.a: The uncle probably saw a lot of effort without action and asked out of concern, hoping Kiran would take a first step.

grounding: Shows a young professional filling notebooks with plans without starting, so writing feels like progress while nothing begins.

subtype: Approach: reviews the page and circles one next action [Revision]
passage:
'That's four notebooks of ideas, Leena,' Vikas said, tapping the table. 'When does the newsletter launch?'

Leena laughed weakly. 'When I finish planning it.'

'Which part is the hard one?'

'All of it.' She turned pages, then stopped with the pen in her hand. 'No, that's not true. Nearly all of this is fine. The only thing blocking me is the sign-up form, and I've drawn it three times.'

'So?'

'So...' She circled it in red. 'Tomorrow, nine-thirty, build the form. Just the form.' She wrote 9:30 beside the circle.

'And the other pages?'

'They can wait.' She closed the notebook. 'At nine-thirty I open the laptop, not the notebook.'

qa.q: What did Leena circle in red?
qa.a: Leena circled the sign-up form.

qa.q: How was Leena feeling at the start of the conversation?
qa.a: Leena felt stuck and a little embarrassed, since she laughed weakly and said the launch would come when she finished planning.

qa.q: What could Leena do if the form takes longer than expected?
qa.a: Leena could build a simpler version of the form, or set a second time slot tomorrow afternoon for the rest.

qa.q: How might Vikas see Leena's decision?
qa.a: Vikas may feel relieved and encouraged to see the notebooks turned into one concrete task.

grounding: Shows a person reviewing plans, circling one step doable tomorrow and putting a time beside it.

subtype: Approach: gives a part of the task to someone who can do it [Action]
passage:
Monday. Nikhil was in charge of Friday's class quiz, and Miss Elizabeth had said he could choose how to do it. He wrote "questions", "score chart" and "prizes" on a page, and felt a knot in his stomach. Too much for one person. In the corridor he noticed Bhavna's notebook, with letters as tidy as print. "Will you make the score chart? I'll do the questions." "Yes," said Bhavna.

Wednesday. Nikhil had twenty questions ready. Bhavna showed him a chart with four team columns and empty boxes. "Is it big enough?" "Add a column for bonus points," said Nikhil.

Friday. The chart hung on the board, and Bhavna filled in the scores after each round while Nikhil read out the questions. Miss Elizabeth clapped.

qa.q: What did Nikhil ask Bhavna to make?
qa.a: Nikhil asked Bhavna to make the score chart.

qa.q: How was Nikhil feeling on Monday when he looked at the page?
qa.a: Nikhil felt overwhelmed, with a knot in his stomach, because it was too much for one person.

qa.q: What could Nikhil do to check that handing over the chart works well?
qa.a: Nikhil could look at the chart midweek, as he did, and agree what to do if Bhavna needs help.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have felt about being asked?
qa.a: Bhavna may have felt pleased and trusted, because her tidy writing had been noticed.

grounding: Shows a boy asking a neat-writing friend to make the score chart while he prepares the quiz questions.
